weeks.title: (Mis)Alignment Through Reinforcement Learning
weeks.description: This week, we examine the interaction between alignment and reinforcement learning. First, we will learn about reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), one of the earliest and most important alignment techniques. We will study it in technical depth, including PPO, the reinforcement learning algorithm it commonly uses. Next, we will read a paper showing that LLMs tend to echo users' political views, a form of sycophancy that is partly caused by RLHF. We will conclude with two papers on how reinforcement can go wrong. The first shows how reward hacking can teach models harmful behavior, and the second shows how reinforcement learning can produce models that chase rewards while ignoring what their developers intended. The goal of this week is to understand the ways in which reinforcement learning can be both a solution and a risk for alignment.

articles.title: Recent Developments in AI
articles.html:
Trump and top AI leaders agree to voluntary ​AI ​standards

September 29, 2026

On September 29, Six prominent tech executives met with Donald Trump at the White House and signed an accord with him on AI standards. It commits companies to four layers of oversight: internal monitoring of model capabilities and alignment, internal teams focused on control measures, independent external auditors, and a board committee that reviews the findings and makes sure problems are fixed. House Speaker Mike Johnson called the accord a statement of voluntary industry commitments, as it lists no consequences for a company that doesn't comply. At the same event, Trump signed an executive order, "Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence," directing federal agencies to replace "Artificial Intelligence" and "AI" with "Super Intelligence" and "SI" in official communications.

OpenAI announces more advancements in mathematics

October 6, 2026

OpenAI released 722 math papers written by an unreleased internal model, kept from about 4,000 open problems it attempted. The headline claims:

  • Riemann Hypothesis progress: a large zero-free region for the zeta function, giving much sharper control over prime distribution.
  • Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer, a Millennium Prize problem, proved for a large class of elliptic curves.
  • An Erdős conjecture: any set of whole numbers whose reciprocals sum to infinity contains evenly spaced patterns (like 5, 9, 13, 17) of every length.
  • Counterexamples to long-standing conjectures in graph theory and algebra.

Here was OpenAI’s announcement:

We’re releasing a broad range of new mathematical results produced by an internal frontier model.

As we look to improve how we share results with the math community, we’ve been consulting with the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study⁠ to develop best practices, and we have drawn on their advice and public recommendations to inform how we release these results.

For this release, we’re publishing the results in a GitHub repository, with protocols for paper revisions and citations. We’re continuing to explore other community-hosted alternatives for this release which meet the committee’s guidelines. For future releases, we are committed to further improving the quality of the papers via the citations, mathematical exposition, and presentation of the results for better understanding.

As part of our GitHub repository, we are sharing formalizations of many of the proofs in Lean, a programming language that allows mathematical proofs to be checked by a computer. We will update the repository with more formalizations as we obtain them.

To promote scientific transparency and openness, we are also publishing additional details about how we obtained the results in the repository. These include 10 summaries of the model’s reasoning, estimations of compute spent in terms of Pro usage on ChatGPT, and statistics about the number of attempted problems. The average result used the equivalent compute of roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking.

We want this progress to push the frontier of human knowledge and enable further progress in mathematics. We will be funding a series of workshops, conferences, and special programs around the understanding of major results produced by AI—we will share more on this in the near future.

We want to directly empower scientists with state-of-the-art capabilities and are working to responsibly release the model that produced these results. This is why it is important to continue to evaluate our internal frontier models on mathematics and other sciences, so we can accelerate developing the tools to advance those fields. We will continue to act on feedback from the community and update our standards for future disclosures of major scientific advancements.
